label: Tool-grounded rewards for RTL generation
lesson:
# Tool-grounded rewards for RTL generation

Training models to write RTL with reinforcement learning needs a reward, and the most reliable rewards come from tools: compilers, simulators, equivalence checkers and synthesis. A tool-grounded reward is deterministic and checkable, but every tool has blind spots, and a model optimized hard against them will find them. Designing the reward is therefore an exercise in knowing exactly what each tool does and does not check.

## Components of a grounded reward

A tool-grounded reward scores generated RTL with deterministic tools against a ground truth: does it compile, does it pass a held-out testbench or prove equivalent to a reference, does it synthesize without latches or errors, and what area and timing does synthesis report. Each component measures something different. Compile success is necessary but nearly worthless alone, because a module that outputs zero compiles, and a model rewarded only for compiling learns to emit safe, useless code.

Correctness needs a reference behavior, from tests or from equivalence checking, and quality terms must be gated on correctness. If smaller area scores higher regardless, the model learns to delete functionality the tests do not exercise.

## Reward hacking

A model maximizes what the reward measures, not what was meant. If the testbench is visible during generation, the model can special-case the stimulus. If it learns that adding a full_case pragma reduces area while the simulation tests still pass, it exploits a gap between the synthesis assumption and the simulation check. If simulation is two-state, a register with no reset reaching an output never shows as x, so the missing reset goes unpunished.

Each hack points at a defense. Regenerate constrained random stimulus for every evaluation so that memorizing it does not help; add formal checks where a reference exists; check four-state behavior or randomize initial values; lint for pragmas and other constructs that change synthesis semantics without being checked. The reward is only as honest as its least careful checker.

## Fast proxies and signoff

Accurate evaluation is expensive. Full place-and-route and signoff timing for every sample would make training unaffordable, so rewards use fast proxies, such as Yosys area estimates or a quick timing estimate. The gap between proxy and signoff quality is where optimization drifts: a model can learn structures that score well on the proxy and poorly after routing.

Two practices contain the drift. Periodically evaluate a sample of outputs with the accurate flow and check that proxy improvements still track real ones, the same fast-versus-accurate pattern used in design loops. Version and pin every tool in the reward, because a tool update that changes results for identical outputs corrupts the learning signal. For benchmarks, tasks drawn from real modules with hidden tests and synthesis checks separate useful models far better than short textbook exercises or prompts that include their own tests.

## Going deeper

The agent-first EDA notes in this curriculum on tool-grounded reinforcement learning; published RTL-generation benchmarks with hidden testbenches.

problems.q:
Which reward for training an RTL-generating model is grounded in tools rather than in a model's opinion?

A) A second model's rating of code style

B) The model's own confidence

C) The length of the generated code

D) A score built from compile success, hidden-test pass rate and synthesis results on the generated RTL
problems.a: A score built from compile success, hidden-test pass rate and synthesis results on the generated RTL
problems.e: Tool-grounded rewards come from deterministic tools judging the output against ground truth.

problems.q:
A reward adds synthesized area so that smaller designs score higher. Which risk appears?

A) Synthesis always increases area

B) The model may delete functionality that the tests do not exercise, shrinking area at the cost of correctness

C) Area cannot be measured

D) The model learns to add registers
problems.a: The model may delete functionality that the tests do not exercise, shrinking area at the cost of correctness
problems.e: Quality terms must be gated on correctness, or the cheapest design wins.

problems.q:
Which reward component directly measures functional correctness of generated RTL?

A) Simulation run time

B) Pass rate on a held-out testbench or a formal equivalence result against a reference

C) Lint warning count

D) Cell count after synthesis
problems.a: Pass rate on a held-out testbench or a formal equivalence result against a reference
problems.e: Correctness needs a reference behavior; tests and equivalence provide it.

problems.q:
A model learns to add the full_case pragma everywhere. Tests still pass and area drops. What kind of problem is this?

A) A compiler bug

B) Overfitting to lint

C) Reward hacking: the pragma changes synthesis assumptions without the simulation tests checking them

D) A legitimate optimization in all cases
problems.a: Reward hacking: the pragma changes synthesis assumptions without the simulation tests checking them
problems.e: The model exploits a gap between what the reward measures (sim tests, area) and what is wanted (correct hardware).

problems.q:
Which defense makes a functional-correctness reward hard to game by hard-coding outputs?

A) Only checking compile success

B) Checking the code length

C) Constrained random stimulus regenerated for every evaluation, plus formal checks where a reference exists

D) A fixed set of ten directed tests
problems.a: Constrained random stimulus regenerated for every evaluation, plus formal checks where a reference exists
problems.e: If the stimulus changes every time, memorizing it does not help.

problems.q:
A model's RTL passes simulation with a two-state simulator but contains a register with no reset whose value reaches an output. Why might the reward not notice?

A) Two-state simulation gives the register a concrete initial value, so the missing reset never shows as x

B) Registers are not simulated

C) The reward measures area only

D) Outputs are not compared
problems.a: Two-state simulation gives the register a concrete initial value, so the missing reset never shows as x
problems.e: The checker's own blind spots become exploitable; adding four-state or randomized-init checks closes this one.

problems.q:
A reward uses Yosys area estimates while the real target is post-route timing and area. What is this gap?

A) A sign that the proxy is useless

B) The difference between a fast proxy reward and signoff quality, which RL can exploit

C) A guarantee of equal results

D) An equivalence failure
problems.a: The difference between a fast proxy reward and signoff quality, which RL can exploit
problems.e: Fast proxies make training affordable, but optimizing them hard can drift away from the true objective.

problems.q:
Why should reward evaluation tools be versioned and pinned during a training run?

A) A change in a tool's behavior would change the reward for identical outputs and corrupt the learning signal

B) Because newer tools are always worse

C) Because tools are slow to download

D) Because rewards must be random
problems.a: A change in a tool's behavior would change the reward for identical outputs and corrupt the learning signal
problems.e: Deterministic, reproducible reward computation is part of grounding.

problems.q:
Which benchmark property best separates RTL-generating models that are genuinely useful?

A) Tasks drawn from real modules with hidden tests and synthesis checks, not short textbook exercises

B) Very short prompts with one-line answers

C) Tasks whose tests are given in the prompt

D) Tasks graded by compile success only
problems.a: Tasks drawn from real modules with hidden tests and synthesis checks, not short textbook exercises
problems.e: Generic coding benchmarks under-separate models on real engineering tasks; realistic, hidden checks do better.

prereqs: Engines as agent tools over MCP
lesson:
# LLM-friendly hardware IRs

An agent that edits hardware can work on Verilog text, on a netlist IR or on a structured compiler IR. The choice matters: some representations make edits local, explicit and checkable, while others hide meaning in implicit rules and distant context. This concept asks what makes an IR friendly to language models, and how tools should expose it to them.

## Properties that make edits safe

Four properties make an IR easier for a model to edit correctly. A textual form that round-trips exactly, so the model reads and writes the same thing the compiler holds. Explicit types and widths on every value, so an edit can be checked without reconstructing context from declarations far away. SSA form, so each value has one definition and the effect of a change can be traced through explicit uses. And a strict parser and verifier that report the offending operation and the expected type, turning a malformed edit into immediate, actionable feedback.

Stable, source-derived names complete the list. They let the agent relate an IR value to the RTL signal it came from and to the timing or lint report that mentions it, which is what makes acting on a report possible.

## Comparing hardware representations

Verilog is what humans write, but its implicit rules (expression sizing, signedness, blocking order, preprocessor macros) are exactly where edits silently go wrong. A structural IR such as CIRCT's hw and comb dialects has none of them: each operation has one meaning, widths are explicit and signless integers remove signedness ambiguity. MLIR adds declarative operation definitions with verifiers and a pattern-rewriting framework, giving a structured way to express transformations.

Lower levels serve algorithms, not editors. An and-inverter graph is ideal for logic optimization but is bit-level and anonymous, so the designer's intent and word structure are gone. RTLIL sits between: word-level cells with source attributes, readable and round-trippable, close to what synthesis sees. For a 200,000-line design, the representation matters less than retrieval: a query tool that returns the relevant operations and their neighborhood beats pasting the whole design into a prompt.

## Exposing IR edits as tools

Free-text patches to IR can be malformed in ways the model cannot see. A typed tool interface, for example over MCP, offers operations such as replace operand, insert operation or rename value, validated by the tool before they touch the IR. This is a seam: the model chooses edits, the tool guarantees their well-formedness.

Well-formed is not correct. An edit that passes the verifier proves only structural validity, not that the design still computes the intended function, so equivalence checks or tests still follow. The easiest proposals to verify are small: a local rewrite pattern with a stated precondition can be proven by an equivalence tool on small instances or tested exhaustively, while a rewritten whole design cannot be checked as cheaply. Explicit dataflow, where every dependence is a visible operand rather than shared mutable state, keeps an edit's reach computable from its uses.

## Going deeper

Lattner et al., "MLIR: Scaling Compiler Infrastructure for Domain Specific Computation" (CGO 2021); the CIRCT rationale documents; the Model Context Protocol specification.

problems.q:
Which property makes an IR easier for a language model to edit safely?

A) A binary-only format

B) Names that change on every dump

C) A textual form that round-trips exactly, with explicit types and widths on every value

D) Implicit widths inferred from distant context
problems.a: A textual form that round-trips exactly, with explicit types and widths on every value
problems.e: Explicit local information lets an edit be checked without reconstructing global context.

problems.q:
Why are stable, source-derived names in an IR useful for agents?

A) They hide the design

B) They make the IR run faster

C) They let the agent relate an IR value to the RTL signal and to reports that mention it

D) They are required by SSA
problems.a: They let the agent relate an IR value to the RTL signal and to reports that mention it
problems.e: Traceability between source, IR and reports is what lets an agent act on a timing or lint report.

problems.q:
An agent edits MLIR text and introduces a type mismatch. What catches it immediately?

A) Only a full simulation

B) The parser and verifier, which report the operation and the expected type

C) The operating system

D) Nothing until synthesis
problems.a: The parser and verifier, which report the operation and the expected type
problems.e: A strict verifier with precise messages turns a malformed edit into fast, actionable feedback.

problems.q:
Compared with raw Verilog, what does an agent gain by editing a structural IR such as CIRCT's hw and comb?

A) Built-in timing closure

B) Shorter text in every case

C) Automatic test generation

D) No preprocessor, no implicit sizing rules and no procedural ambiguity: each operation has one meaning
problems.a: No preprocessor, no implicit sizing rules and no procedural ambiguity: each operation has one meaning
problems.e: Verilog's implicit rules (sizing, signedness, blocking order) are where edits silently go wrong; a structural IR makes them explicit.

problems.q:
Why is an AIG a poor format for an agent to edit by hand, even though it is ideal for logic optimization?

A) It is not a graph

B) It cannot be stored as text

C) It contains no logic

D) It is bit-level and anonymous, so the designer's intent and the word structure are gone
problems.a: It is bit-level and anonymous, so the designer's intent and the word structure are gone
problems.e: Low-level IRs are for algorithms; edits that reflect intent belong at a level that still shows it.

problems.q:
An agent must change one comparison in a 200,000-line design. What helps most?

A) A query tool that returns the relevant operations and their neighborhood instead of the whole IR

B) Pasting the whole design into the prompt

C) Reading it file by file in order

D) Converting the design to an AIG first
problems.a: A query tool that returns the relevant operations and their neighborhood instead of the whole IR
problems.e: Large designs exceed any context window; retrieval of the relevant slice keeps edits focused.

problems.q:
A team wants agents to propose optimizations as IR rewrites. Which form of proposal is easiest to verify?

A) A natural-language description

B) A local rewrite pattern with a stated precondition, checkable by an equivalence tool on small instances

C) A new compiler built from scratch

D) A rewritten whole design
problems.a: A local rewrite pattern with a stated precondition, checkable by an equivalence tool on small instances
problems.e: Small, local rewrites can be proven or exhaustively tested; whole-design rewrites cannot be checked as cheaply.

problems.q:
Which IR property most reduces the chance that a model's edit has a non-local effect it did not see?

A) Implicit sensitivity lists

B) Global variables

C) Textual macros

D) Explicit dataflow, where every dependence is a visible operand rather than a shared mutable variable
problems.a: Explicit dataflow, where every dependence is a visible operand rather than a shared mutable variable
problems.e: When all dependences are explicit, an edit's reach can be computed from its uses.

problems.q:
An agent's IR edit passes the verifier. What does that prove?

A) That the design is correct

B) That the IR is well-formed, not that it computes the intended function

C) That the edit is minimal

D) That timing is met
problems.a: That the IR is well-formed, not that it computes the intended function
problems.e: Structural validity and semantic correctness are separate; equivalence or tests are still needed.

# MLIR and CIRCT as an agent-editable compiler

MLIR and CIRCT, and Yosys with its plug-in passes, are compilers designed to be extended. Mapping them onto the four-layer engine model shows where an agent's changes belong: configuration, plug-in passes and patterns, or the rarely touched core of IR semantics. This concept makes that mapping concrete, with change tiers, seams and the checks that promote an agent-written pass into a reusable skill.

## The four layers of a hardware compiler

The immutable core of a CIRCT-based compiler is the dialect definitions, the meaning of each operation and the verifier; every pass and lowering is written against them, so changing them is a core change. The strategy or policy layer is the passes and rewrite patterns, which decide how a design is transformed and are chosen, ordered and added without changing the IR's meaning. The parameter layer is pass options and the pipeline description: thresholds, modes, which passes run in which order. The observation layer is pass instrumentation and IR dumps before and after chosen passes, where an agent watches the compiler's state.

Yosys maps the same way: RTLIL data structures and internal cell semantics are the core, passes are policy, synthesis script options (whether to flatten, which ABC script to run) are parameters, and logs and write_rtlil dumps are observation hooks.

## Which tier a request lands in

A request to reorder existing passes is Tier 1, configuration: MLIR pass pipelines can be written textually, so no recompile is needed. A request for a new peephole rewrite, such as turning a multiplexer of two constants into an XOR, is Tier 2: a plug-in pattern registered at the dialect's extension point, leaving operation definitions untouched. Adding a Yosys pass as a loadable plug-in rather than patching Yosys sources is also Tier 2.

A request that changes what an operation means, such as the overflow behavior of comb.add, is Tier 3: a core edit, needing human approval and full regression of every pass that relied on the old meaning. Customer-specific policy, such as mapping wide multipliers to a particular DSP macro, belongs in a plug-in lowering pattern selected by configuration, never in the core lowering of the multiply operation, so the core stays shared and stable.

## Seams, checks and promotion

A rewrite pattern is a good seam for agent-written changes: small, local, independently testable and applied by a trusted driver that keeps the IR well-formed. What it may break is confined to the operations it matches. The differential check for a new pattern must prove two things: that each rewrite preserves the function of the matched operations, for example with an equivalence check over the before and after IR, and that quality on reference designs moves only as intended.

Once those checks pass, the pattern can be promoted from an experiment into a library skill. What makes it reusable is a manifest stating what it does, its inputs and outputs and its tunable options, plus its golden and differential tests. Other agents then select it by reading the manifest, without reading its source, and the tests keep it trustworthy as the compiler evolves.

## Going deeper

The MLIR documentation on pattern rewriting, dialect conversion and pass pipelines; the Yosys manual on writing and loading plug-in passes; the agent-first EDA notes in this curriculum.

problems.q:
In that model, what is the strategy or policy layer of a hardware compiler?

A) The MLIR parser

B) The operation definitions

C) The command-line flag values

D) The passes and rewrite patterns, which decide how the design is transformed
problems.a: The passes and rewrite patterns, which decide how the design is transformed
problems.e: Passes are policies: they are chosen, ordered and added without changing the IR's meaning.

problems.q:
In the four-layer engine model applied to a CIRCT-based compiler, which part is the immutable core?

A) The IR dumps an agent reads

B) The order of passes in the pipeline

C) Dialect definitions, operation semantics and the verifier

D) Pass options such as thresholds
problems.a: Dialect definitions, operation semantics and the verifier
problems.e: Everything else is built on what operations mean; changing that is a core change needing review and full regression.

problems.q:
Which item belongs to the parameter layer of a Yosys-based flow?

A) The RTLIL data structures

B) A new C++ pass

C) The synthesis script's options, such as whether to flatten or which ABC script to run

D) The definition of the add cell
problems.a: The synthesis script's options, such as whether to flatten or which ABC script to run
problems.e: Parameters change behavior with no recompile: script options, pass flags, thresholds.

problems.q:
A request requires changing what comb.add means for overflow. Which tier is this, and what follows?

A) Tier 1, a flag

B) Tier 3, a core edit, which needs human approval and full regression of every pass that relies on the old meaning

C) Tier 2, a pattern

D) No change is needed
problems.a: Tier 3, a core edit, which needs human approval and full regression of every pass that relies on the old meaning
problems.e: Semantics are the core: every pattern and lowering was written against them.

problems.q:
A user asks for a different pass order in an MLIR-based flow, using passes that already exist. Which change tier is this?

A) Tier 3: a core edit

B) Tier 1: configuration, a pipeline description change with no recompile

C) Not a change at all

D) Tier 2: a plug-in
problems.a: Tier 1: configuration, a pipeline description change with no recompile
problems.e: Pass pipelines can be specified textually, so reordering existing passes is pure configuration.

problems.q:
A user wants a new peephole rewrite that turns a mux of two constants into an XOR. Which tier is this?

A) Tier 3: a new parser

B) Tier 3: a change to the comb dialect's semantics

C) Tier 1: a flag change

D) Tier 2: a plug-in rewrite pattern registered at the dialect's extension point
problems.a: Tier 2: a plug-in rewrite pattern registered at the dialect's extension point
problems.e: New patterns extend the policy layer without touching operation definitions.

problems.q:
What must the differential check for a new rewrite pattern prove?

A) That the IR prints

B) That the pattern compiles

C) That each rewrite preserves the function of the matched operations, for example by an equivalence check, and that QoR on reference designs moves only as intended

D) That the pattern fires at least once
problems.a: That each rewrite preserves the function of the matched operations, for example by an equivalence check, and that QoR on reference designs moves only as intended
problems.e: Correctness of the rewrite and its effect on quality are both part of promoting it.

problems.q:
Why is a rewrite pattern a good seam for agent-written compiler changes?

A) It can change any part of the compiler

B) It is small, local, independently testable and applied by a trusted driver that keeps the IR well-formed

C) It runs before parsing

D) It needs no tests
problems.a: It is small, local, independently testable and applied by a trusted driver that keeps the IR well-formed
problems.e: A narrow interface with a trusted applicator confines what an agent's code can break.

problems.q:
Where should a customer-specific lowering rule, such as 'map wide multipliers to our DSP macro', live?

A) In the verifier

B) In the definition of the multiply operation

C) In a plug-in lowering pattern selected by configuration, not in the core lowering of the multiply operation

D) In the parser
problems.a: In a plug-in lowering pattern selected by configuration, not in the core lowering of the multiply operation
problems.e: Customer-specific policy belongs at the change surface, so the core stays shared and stable.
